study_identification_part.si4_title: A multimodal neural signature of face processing in autism within the fusiform gyrus

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To provide a comprehensive understanding of the fusiform gyrus (FFG) in face processing in autism by elucidating the simultaneous involvement and multivariate interplay of different neural sources across structural MRI, resting-state fMRI, task-fMRI and EEG. The study combined normative modeling and linked independent component analysis to assess how multimodal components differentiated groups and informed social functioning in autism.

rci8_quality_checking.detail: Multiple QC procedures implemented: (1) Structural T1: CAT12-derived weighted overall image quality ratings (0.5 best to 10.5 worst); excluded images with excessive head motion (N=37), clinically non-significant atypicalities (N=21), failed preprocessing (N=3); groups matched on quality measures after exclusions (W=4926, p=0.52). (2) Rs-fMRI: excluded scans with <180 volumes (N=8), excessive motion (meanFD >0.7mm N=29; maxFD >7.6mm N=38), low coverage (N=24), extreme values >4SD (N=12), failed preprocessing (N=1); groups matched on meanFD after exclusions (W=4915, p=0.5). (3) Task-fMRI: excluded scans with excessive motion (>20% trials meanFD >0.5mm; N=47); groups matched on motion after exclusions (W=5279, p=0.83). (4) EEG: excluded technical/upload errors (N=33), incomplete battery (N=32), <20 artifact-free trials (N=9), <75% channels (N=2). Both automated metrics and visual inspection performed.

rci9_site_effect_handling.detail: Site was included as a covariate in Bayesian linear regression normative models alongside age and sex. Site-specific effects were modeled during normative modeling estimation. No separate batch-removal harmonization (like ComBat) was applied prior to modeling. Multi-site data acquisition used harmonized protocols and quality assurance procedures with phantoms and traveling heads to ensure standardization across six acquisition sites (KCL, RUNMC, UCAM, UMCU, UCBM, CIMH). Site effects were also tested in group comparisons showing no significant site × diagnosis interactions for IC44.

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Z-scores derived from normative models quantifying individual-level deviations from predicted age-, sex-, and site-adjusted trajectories. For group comparisons of extreme deviations: absolute threshold |Z| > 2.6 (corresponding to p < 0.005, 99.5th percentile). Percentage of extreme positive and negative deviations per individual calculated relative to total voxels/timepoints. For multimodal analysis: unthresholded Z-deviation maps were used as features for LICA to derive multimodal components.
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The methods section clearly describes how deviations were quantified using Z-scores from normative models, and how extreme deviations were defined for statistical comparisons.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: To estimate voxel-wise/time point-wise deviations for each modality in each individual, we derived normative probability maps (NPM) that quantify the deviation from the normative model summarized in Z-scores. These subject-specific Z-score images provide a statistical estimate of how much each individual's recorded value differs from the predicted value at each voxel/time point. ... Finally, to assess whether autistic and non-autistic individuals differed in their extreme deviations, the NPMs were thresholded at an absolute value of Z>|2.6| (i.e., p < 0.005). Based on this fixed threshold, we defined extreme positive and extreme negative deviations for each participant. All extreme deviations per individual were summarized into scores representing the percentage of extreme positive and extreme negative deviations per individual in relation to the total number of voxels.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Group differences in multimodal independent components (ICs) tested using two-sample t-tests with FDR correction for multiple comparisons. Normality tested with Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and equal variances with Levene's test. Support vector machine (SVM) classification with linear kernel under 10-fold cross-validation to compare discrimination ability of multimodal vs unimodal ICs; class weighting for group imbalance; AUC as performance metric; permutation testing (10,000 iterations) to test significance of AUC differences. Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) to model multivariate relationship between multimodal ICs and clinical/cognitive features; Huh-Jhun residualization for age, sex, site; complete permutation inference (10,000 iterations) for significance testing; stepwise cumulative maximum approach for multiple comparison correction (p<0.05); Haufe transformation for interpretable loadings. Sensitivity analyses across varying multimodality thresholds (85-99%). Additional control analyses for handedness (Spearman correlations, covariate inclusion, exclusion of left-handed/ambidextrous). Brain-behavior correlations visualized using correlations between original Z-deviation maps and CCA canonical imaging variates (1,000 permutations for significance). Spatial characterization via overlap with Harvard-Oxford and VIS atlases.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Autistic individuals showed significant differences in a multimodal component (IC44) driven by bilateral resting-state fMRI, bilateral structure, right task-fMRI and left EEG within face-selective and retinotopic regions of the fusiform gyrus; multimodal components outperformed unimodal ones in group classification (AUC 0.64 vs 0.48, p<0.001) and were specifically associated with social but not nonsocial functioning measures in autism.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Among 50 independent components, one multimodal IC (IC44) showed significant group difference with autistic individuals having higher contributions than controls (t=3.5, pFDR=0.027). This component was driven by rs-fMRI (48.5% right, 35.0% left), EEG left (11.6%), task-fMRI right (3.3%), and GM volume (1.0% right, 0.5% left). In the right hemisphere, autistic individuals showed linked increased deviations in rs-fMRI and structure primarily in higher-order face-selective (mFus, pFus/FFA-1, FFA-2) and body-selective regions, while showing decreased deviations in rs-fMRI and task-fMRI in FFA and retinotopic regions. In the left hemisphere, increased rs-fMRI connectivity deviations were found in retinotopic and lower-order face regions, with decreased deviations in structure and rs-fMRI in face-selective and retinotopic areas. EEG showed increased left source activation at 195-203ms and 417-426ms, and decreased activation at 444-449ms. SVM classification showed multimodal ICs (AUC=0.64) significantly outperformed unimodal ICs (AUC=0.48, p<0.001). CCA revealed significant multivariate association between multimodal ICs and social-communicative features (r=0.65, pFDR=0.008), with IC37, IC38, IC44, and IC34 contributing most on imaging side, and ADOS social affect, RMET, and Hariri faces contributing most on behavioral side. Joint imaging patterns showed both increased and decreased deviations in face-selective and retinotopic regions across modalities, associated with more social difficulties (ADOS, ADI, Vineland), more RMET errors, but greater Hariri faces accuracy. No significant association was found with nonsocial features including RRBs (r=0.45, pFDR=0.64), demonstrating specificity to social functioning.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: The study focused on the fusiform gyrus in isolation despite face processing involving an extended network including amygdala, superior temporal sulcus, and occipital/frontal cortex. Multi-site data collection required harmonization despite using standardized protocols. From over 600 LEAP participants, only 204 had complete data across all four modalities, limiting sample size for multimodal analyses and preventing sex-stratified analyses due to small female sample. Small number of left-handed/ambidextrous participants limited ability to examine handedness effects on face processing lateralization. Choice of geometric shapes as comparison stimuli rather than face-like stimuli may affect face-specificity of task-based findings. EEG used generic electrode positions and head models with lower spatial resolution compared to fMRI. Analyses combined upright and inverted faces to maintain sample size and signal-to-noise ratio.
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: At the same time, it needs to be pointed out that face processing involves an extended neural network across the whole brain, including other structures such as the amygdala, superior temporal sulcus and occipital and frontal cortex. ... Additionally, implementing cross-modal analyses presents additional challenges, such as obtaining sufficiently large sample sizes with all participants having available data across all imaging modalities. Here, from a sample of over 600 individuals in the EU-AIMS LEAP dataset, we were able to conduct an analysis in just over 200 individuals who had available imaging data across the four different modalities. ... although our prior work suggests that face processing is related to sex-differential factors in autism, in the current study we did not run sex-stratified analyses owing to the small number of female participants. ... Owing to the small number of left-handed or ambidextrous individuals in our sample, it is not surprising that we did not find an association with handedness. ... Comparison stimuli vary in the degree to which they resemble living objects or faces ... choice of comparison stimuli is a limitation, which may affect the face specificity of task-based findings.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study innovatively combined two methodological approaches: (1) normative modeling to derive individual-level deviations accounting for age/sex/site, and (2) linked independent component analysis (LICA) for multimodal fusion. LICA was chosen for its ability to handle modalities with different numbers of features, spatial correlations, intensity distributions, and units by optimally weighting contributions through correction for effective degrees of freedom and automatic relevance determination priors. Hemispheres were modeled separately to study hemispheric contributions and account for different noise characteristics. Multimodal index (MMI) was calculated to quantify the multimodal nature of each IC, with threshold of 0.1 (no single modality >90%) used to define multimodal components. Spatial characterization used overlap with both anatomical (Harvard-Oxford atlas) and functional (VIS probabilistic atlas of occipito-temporal cortex) atlases to characterize fine-grained topography. The study demonstrated specificity by testing associations with both social-communicative and nonsocial feature sets separately. Clinical data imputation was performed using Extra Trees regression to handle missing data without reducing sample size. Face processing analyses combined upright and inverted faces as no group×orientation interaction was found for N170.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a multimodal neuroimaging study combining structural MRI, rs-fMRI, task-fMRI, and EEG with normative modeling and linked ICA. The study is part of the large-scale EU-AIMS/AIMS-2-TRIALS LEAP consortium involving six sites across Europe (KCL, RUNMC, UCAM, UMCU, UCBM, CIMH). Age range spans from childhood to adulthood (7-30 years). The study used gold-standard diagnostic instruments (ADI-R and ADOS) to confirm autism diagnosis. Most participants were Caucasian white (74.5%). Medication use was allowed if stable for ≥8 weeks (30-50% of autistic participants on medication, see Supplementary Table 11). EEG data were not collected at Cambridge site; rs-fMRI data were not collected at Rome site. Three different EEG systems were used across sites (Brainproducts Acticaps, Biosemi Active-Two, Micromed). Rs-fMRI used multi-echo EPI sequence. The Hariri task used fearful/angry emotional faces contrasted with geometric shapes. FFG ROI was defined from four Harvard-Oxford atlas regions (anterior/posterior temporal fusiform cortex, temporal-occipital fusiform cortex, occipital fusiform gyrus) and adjusted for 100% coverage across rs-fMRI scans. Individual FFA peaks were identified within mFus and pFus regions for seed-based connectivity. For EEG, FFG was downsampled to 18 cortical parcels per hemisphere due to lower spatial resolution. Model order of 50 ICs was selected based on sample size (N/4). Robustness analyses tested alternative model orders (40, 60) and multimodality thresholds (85-99%). Code availability: normative modeling (PCNtoolkit on GitHub), LICA (GitHub), CCA (PermCCA on GitHub). Data available through application process. Published in Nature Mental Health, 2025 (received Feb 2024, accepted Oct 2024, published online Jan 2025).
